521	/// Builds the `MTAudioProcessingTap` for one composition audio track.
522	enum AudioTap {
523	    /// nil when the track needs no processing AND is not being metered, or
524	    /// when MediaToolbox refuses to make a tap — in which case the track plays
525	    /// and exports unprocessed and unmetered, which is the old behaviour
526	    /// rather than a failed build.
527	    ///
528	    /// A `meter` alone is enough to earn a tap: a metering build wants a level
529	    /// from every audio track, including the ones no clip has asked anything
530	    /// of. That tap builds no chain and touches no sample — it fetches its
531	    /// source audio, hands it straight on, and measures it.
532	    static func make(for track: AudioTrackDSP?, meter: LevelMeterSink?) -> MTAudioProcessingTap? {
533	        let track = track ?? .inert
534	        guard track.isActive || meter != nil else { return nil }
535	        // Retained here, released in `finalize` (or below, if no tap is made):
536	        // the tap owns the context and outlives every Swift reference to it.
537	        let context = Unmanaged.passRetained(
538	            AudioTapContext(track: track, meter: meter)).toOpaque()
539	        var callbacks = MTAudioProcessingTapCallbacks(
540	            version: kMTAudioProcessingTapCallbacksVersion_0,
541	            clientInfo: context,
542	            init: { _, clientInfo, storageOut in storageOut.pointee = clientInfo },
543	            finalize: { tap in
544	                Unmanaged<AudioTapContext>
545	                    .fromOpaque(MTAudioProcessingTapGetStorage(tap)).release()
546	            },
547	            prepare: { tap, maxFrames, format in
548	                let context = Unmanaged<AudioTapContext>
549	                    .fromOpaque(MTAudioProcessingTapGetStorage(tap)).takeUnretainedValue()
550	                context.prepare(
551	                    channelCount: Int(format.pointee.mChannelsPerFrame),
552	                    sampleRate: format.pointee.mSampleRate, maxFrames: Int(maxFrames),
553	                    formatFlags: format.pointee.mFormatFlags,
554	                    bitsPerChannel: format.pointee.mBitsPerChannel)
555	            },
556	            unprepare: { tap in
557	                Unmanaged<AudioTapContext>
558	                    .fromOpaque(MTAudioProcessingTapGetStorage(tap))
559	                    .takeUnretainedValue().unprepare()
560	            },
561	            process: { tap, numberFrames, _, bufferListInOut, numberFramesOut, flagsOut in
562	                let context = Unmanaged<AudioTapContext>
563	                    .fromOpaque(MTAudioProcessingTapGetStorage(tap)).takeUnretainedValue()
564	                var timeRange = CMTimeRange()
565	                // The source audio must be fetched even when nothing will be
566	                // done to it: this call is what hands the buffer on.
567	                guard MTAudioProcessingTapGetSourceAudio(
568	                    tap, numberFrames, bufferListInOut, flagsOut, &timeRange,
569	                    numberFramesOut) == noErr
570	                else {
571	                    numberFramesOut.pointee = 0
572	                    return
573	                }
574	                // `MTAudioProcessingTapFlags` is a plain bit field, not an
575	                // `OptionSet`: the header declares it `uint32_t`.
576	                let startOfStream =
577	                    flagsOut.pointee & MTAudioProcessingTapFlags(
578	                        kMTAudioProcessingTapFlag_StartOfStream) != 0
579	                context.process(
580	                    bufferListInOut, frames: Int(numberFramesOut.pointee),
581	                    time: timeRange.start, startOfStream: startOfStream)
582	            })
583	
584	        var tap: MTAudioProcessingTap?
585	        guard MTAudioProcessingTapCreate(
586	            kCFAllocatorDefault, &callbacks, kMTAudioProcessingTapCreationFlag_PreEffects,
587	            &tap) == noErr
588	        else {
589	            // The context was retained for a tap that does not exist.
590	            Unmanaged<AudioTapContext>.fromOpaque(context).release()
591	            return nil
592	        }
593	        return tap
594	    }

3	import Synchronization

5	/// The level meter's MODEL: what the audio thread measured, how it crosses to
6	/// the main thread, and the arithmetic that turns per-track measurements into
7	/// the one reading a meter draws. No view, no AVFoundation, no AppKit.
8	///
9	/// **Why the meter reads the DSP tap instead of its own.** The road map asked
10	/// for "a second, read-only `MTAudioProcessingTap` per composition track
11	/// created with `kMTAudioProcessingTapCreationFlag_PostEffects`". There is no
12	/// such thing. `AVMutableAudioMixInputParameters` has exactly ONE
13	/// `audioTapProcessor`, and `MTAudioProcessingTap.h` says either the PreEffects
14	/// or the PostEffects flag must be set but not both — so a track already
15	/// carrying the DSP tap (`AudioTap.swift`, PreEffects, deliberately, so the
16	/// compressor sits ahead of the fader) cannot carry a second one, and moving
17	/// the DSP tap to PostEffects would change how every existing project with a
18	/// compressor sounds. So the meter reads the tap that already exists and
19	/// multiplies by the plan's envelope: the tap sees the samples BEFORE volume,
20	/// the fades and ducking, and the envelope at that tick is exactly what
21	/// `CompositionBuilder` hands AVFoundation as volume ramps. The displayed
22	/// number is therefore computed rather than observed, and it is exact rather
23	/// than approximate — the ramps are the same ones AVFoundation is applying.
24	/// `SilenceDetector` already established this as the app's rule ("a peak is
25	/// pre-fader, so the level you want is peak × envelope"). Do not "fix" this
26	/// back toward a second tap; it cannot be built.
27	///
28	/// **Why the publish is lock-free, when everything else in the app is an
29	/// `NSLock`.** `RecipeSource`, `AudioDSPSource`, `ReverseSource`,
30	/// `ExportWriter`'s progress — every cross-thread value in `app/Sources` is a
31	/// lock or a `DispatchQueue.main.async` hop. Neither may be used here.
32	/// `LevelMeterSink.publish` runs inside `MTAudioProcessingTap`'s process
33	/// callback, on AVPlayer's real-time render thread, where `AudioDSP.swift`'s
34	/// stated discipline holds: nothing takes a lock, nothing allocates. A lock
35	/// can block on a lower-priority thread that holds it (priority inversion) and
36	/// a `main.async` allocates, and both fail the same way — an occasional
37	/// glitch nobody can reproduce. So the sink is two 64-bit words written with
38	/// relaxed atomic stores and read the same way: wait-free, no allocation, no
39	/// ordering the render thread has to wait on. This is the app's first
40	/// `import Synchronization`, and it is a deliberate exception of the same
41	/// class as `async` being confined to `MediaImporter.swift`.
42	///
43	/// **The model publishes a RAW measurement; the VIEW owns the ballistics.**
44	/// Peak hold and decay are display behaviour, and keeping them out here is
45	/// what lets a proof assert on the number without photographing a window.
46	///
47	/// **The model is process-wide.** `LevelMeter.shared` is what a meter view
48	/// observes and what `Playback` publishes into, which is what keeps the meter
49	/// out of the frozen `TimelineView`/`EditorViewController` wiring entirely: a
50	/// view subscribes to it directly. With two documents open the meter follows
51	/// whichever transport published last — they share one output device, so
52	/// showing one of them is honest where showing neither is not — with one
53	/// rule that stops the obvious wrong: a SILENT publish from a transport that
54	/// is not the one currently lighting the meter is ignored, so stopping
55	/// playback in window B cannot blank window A's live meter.
56	///
57	/// The units, once: a `LevelMeterReading` is LINEAR magnitude, 1.0 being full
58	/// scale, because that is what the samples are and what multiplies by an
59	/// envelope. dBFS is a computed accessor, floored rather than allowed to reach
60	/// −∞.
61	
62	// MARK: - What is measured
63	
64	/// One measurement: peak and RMS magnitude for two channels, linear.
65	///
66	/// Two channels because the meter has two bars. A mono composition track is
67	/// prepared with one channel and widened downstream of the tap, so its one
68	/// channel is reported in both; a track with more than two (a 5.1 source) is
69	/// reported by its first two, which is what a two-bar meter can honestly say
70	/// about it.
71	struct LevelMeterReading: Equatable {
72	    var peakLeft: Float
73	    var peakRight: Float
74	    var rmsLeft: Float
75	    var rmsRight: Float
76	
77	    init(peakLeft: Float = 0, peakRight: Float = 0, rmsLeft: Float = 0, rmsRight: Float = 0) {
78	        self.peakLeft = LevelMeterReading.sanitised(peakLeft)
79	        self.peakRight = LevelMeterReading.sanitised(peakRight)
80	        // RMS can never exceed peak in one buffer, and the two are read from
81	        // two separate atomic words that may be one buffer apart (see
82	        // `LevelMeterSink`), so the invariant is restored here rather than
83	        // left for the view to draw an RMS fill past the peak tick.
84	        self.rmsLeft = min(LevelMeterReading.sanitised(rmsLeft), self.peakLeft)
85	        self.rmsRight = min(LevelMeterReading.sanitised(rmsRight), self.peakRight)
86	    }
87	
88	    /// A sample that is not a finite number poisons everything downstream —
89	    /// one NaN in a buffer makes the bar vanish and stay vanished — so it is
90	    /// answered as silence, at the one place every value passes through.
91	    private static func sanitised(_ value: Float) -> Float {
92	        guard value.isFinite else { return 0 }
93	        return max(0, value)
94	    }
95	
96	    static let silent = LevelMeterReading()
97	
98	    var isSilent: Bool { peakLeft <= 0 && peakRight <= 0 }
99	
100	    var peakLeftDB: Float { LevelMeterMath.decibels(peakLeft) }
101	    var peakRightDB: Float { LevelMeterMath.decibels(peakRight) }
102	    var rmsLeftDB: Float { LevelMeterMath.decibels(rmsLeft) }
103	    var rmsRightDB: Float { LevelMeterMath.decibels(rmsRight) }
104	
105	    /// The loudest of the two channels' peaks, in dBFS — what a clip
106	    /// indication is decided on.
107	    var peakDB: Float { LevelMeterMath.decibels(max(peakLeft, peakRight)) }
108	
109	    /// This track's contribution, scaled by the mix envelope over it (the
110	    /// volume, fades and ducking the tap ran ahead of).
111	    func scaled(by gain: Float) -> LevelMeterReading {
112	        guard gain.isFinite else { return .silent }
113	        guard gain != 1 else { return self }
114	        let g = max(0, gain)
115	        return LevelMeterReading(
116	            peakLeft: peakLeft * g, peakRight: peakRight * g,
117	            rmsLeft: rmsLeft * g, rmsRight: rmsRight * g)
118	    }
119	
120	    /// Two tracks' readings as one.
121	    ///
122	    /// **Peaks add LINEARLY and RMS adds in POWER**, and the difference is not
123	    /// a nicety. A linear sum of peaks is the arithmetic upper bound on what
124	    /// the mix can reach — the honest thing for a meter whose job is to warn —
125	    /// while adding two RMS values linearly would claim +6 dB for two
126	    /// uncorrelated sources that actually sum to +3. With one audio track,
127	    /// which is most projects, both reduce to the track's own numbers and the
128	    /// distinction never arises.
129	    func adding(_ other: LevelMeterReading) -> LevelMeterReading {
130	        LevelMeterReading(
131	            peakLeft: peakLeft + other.peakLeft,
132	            peakRight: peakRight + other.peakRight,
133	            rmsLeft: (rmsLeft * rmsLeft + other.rmsLeft * other.rmsLeft).squareRoot(),
134	            rmsRight: (rmsRight * rmsRight + other.rmsRight * other.rmsRight).squareRoot())
135	    }
136	}
137	
138	// MARK: - The arithmetic
139	
140	/// The pure pieces: one channel's measurement, and magnitude → dBFS.
141	///
142	/// Separated out so a proof can measure a buffer it authored itself without a
143	/// player, a document or a window anywhere in the picture.
144	enum LevelMeterMath {
145	    /// Where the dB scale bottoms out. −120 dBFS is far under the least
146	    /// significant bit of any 16-bit material, so nothing real is clipped by
147	    /// it; it exists so that `log10(0)` never reaches a layout constraint as
148	    /// −∞ (which lays out as NaN, which AppKit reports as a broken constraint
149	    /// rather than as a silent meter).
150	    static let floorDB: Float = -120
151	
152	    private static let floorLinear: Float = 1e-6  // 10^(-120/20)
153	
154	    /// Peak and RMS of one channel's `frames` samples.
155	    ///
156	    /// `vDSP_maxmgv` and `vDSP_rmsqv` are two linear passes with no allocation
157	    /// and no state, which is what the render thread can afford: at 4096
158	    /// frames this is two orders of magnitude under one noise-reduction frame.
159	    static func measure(_ data: UnsafePointer<Float>, frames: Int) -> (peak: Float, rms: Float) {
160	        guard frames > 0 else { return (0, 0) }
161	        var peak: Float = 0
162	        var rms: Float = 0
163	        vDSP_maxmgv(data, 1, &peak, vDSP_Length(frames))
164	        vDSP_rmsqv(data, 1, &rms, vDSP_Length(frames))
165	        return (peak.isFinite ? peak : 0, rms.isFinite ? rms : 0)
166	    }
167	
168	    /// Linear magnitude → dBFS, floored at `floorDB`. 1.0 is 0 dBFS.
169	    static func decibels(_ magnitude: Float) -> Float {
170	        guard magnitude.isFinite, magnitude > floorLinear else { return floorDB }
171	        return 20 * log10f(magnitude)
172	    }
173	}

175	// MARK: - The crossing

177	/// One composition audio track's meter: written by the tap on the audio
178	/// thread, read by `Playback`'s timer on the main one.
179	///
180	/// **Two words, both relaxed.** Peak L and peak R live in one 64-bit word as
181	/// two `Float` bit patterns; RMS L and RMS R live in the other. One relaxed
182	/// store each per buffer, one relaxed load each per tick. Relaxed is enough
183	/// because there is nothing else to order against: the words carry no
184	/// pointers, publish no other state, and a reader that sees the previous
185	/// buffer's number instead of this one's is showing a meter 1/60 s stale,
186	/// which is invisible. The two words may be one buffer apart from each other
187	/// — `LevelMeterReading.init` restores `rms ≤ peak` for exactly that reason.
188	///
189	/// **One value per BUFFER, not per tick.** `prepare`'s `maxFrames` is about
190	/// 4096 frames — 85 ms — on the paths this app has measured, so the real
191	/// measurement rate is 12–20 Hz and the 30 Hz timer merely re-reads. That is
192	/// what a digital peak meter does; do not read the timer's interval as the
193	/// meter's resolution.
194	final class LevelMeterSink: @unchecked Sendable {
195	    private let peaks = Atomic<UInt64>(0)
196	    private let levels = Atomic<UInt64>(0)
197	
198	    init() {}
199	
200	    /// AUDIO THREAD. Measures one buffer of planar float channels and stores
201	    /// the result. Allocation-free, lock-free, and no read-modify-write: the
202	    /// buffer's own peak IS the value, and the hold and the decay belong to
203	    /// the view.
204	    ///
205	    /// `channels` is the same shape `AudioDSPChain.process` takes — the base
206	    /// pointer of each channel, `frames` samples each — so a proof can drive
207	    /// this with two plain allocations and no player.
208	    func measure(
209	        _ channels: UnsafeMutableBufferPointer<UnsafeMutablePointer<Float>?>, count: Int,
210	        frames: Int
211	    ) {
212	        guard frames > 0, count > 0 else { return }
213	        var left: (peak: Float, rms: Float) = (0, 0)
214	        if let data = channels[0] { left = LevelMeterMath.measure(data, frames: frames) }
215	        // A mono composition track is widened to stereo downstream of the tap,
216	        // so its single channel is what both bars are showing.
217	        var right = left
218	        if count >= 2, let data = channels[1] {
219	            right = LevelMeterMath.measure(data, frames: frames)
220	        }
221	        store(peakLeft: left.peak, peakRight: right.peak, rmsLeft: left.rms, rmsRight: right.rms)
222	    }
223	
224	    /// AUDIO THREAD. The two stores, spelled once.
225	    func store(peakLeft: Float, peakRight: Float, rmsLeft: Float, rmsRight: Float) {
226	        levels.store(Self.pack(rmsLeft, rmsRight), ordering: .relaxed)
227	        // Peak last, so a reader that catches the pair mid-update sees an RMS
228	        // that belongs to an older, quieter buffer rather than a peak that
229	        // does — the direction that under-reports rather than over-reports.
230	        peaks.store(Self.pack(peakLeft, peakRight), ordering: .relaxed)
231	    }
232	
233	    /// MAIN THREAD. The last buffer's measurement.
234	    func read() -> LevelMeterReading {
235	        let p = Self.unpack(peaks.load(ordering: .relaxed))
236	        let r = Self.unpack(levels.load(ordering: .relaxed))
237	        return LevelMeterReading(
238	            peakLeft: p.0, peakRight: p.1, rmsLeft: r.0, rmsRight: r.1)
239	    }
240	
241	    /// Forgets the last buffer, so a resumed preview does not open on the peak
242	    /// it paused at. Two relaxed stores like any other, so it is safe from
243	    /// wherever it is called — the transport calls it on the main thread when
244	    /// playback stops, and the tap calls it from `prepare`/`unprepare` on
245	    /// whichever AVFoundation thread it is handed.
246	    func clear() {
247	        peaks.store(0, ordering: .relaxed)
248	        levels.store(0, ordering: .relaxed)
249	    }
250	
251	    private static func pack(_ high: Float, _ low: Float) -> UInt64 {
252	        UInt64(high.bitPattern) << 32 | UInt64(low.bitPattern)
253	    }
254	
255	    private static func unpack(_ word: UInt64) -> (Float, Float) {
256	        (Float(bitPattern: UInt32(truncatingIfNeeded: word >> 32)),
257	         Float(bitPattern: UInt32(truncatingIfNeeded: word)))
258	    }
259	}

261	/// One metered composition audio track: the sink its tap writes into, the
262	/// envelope that turns what the tap saw into what the mix hears, and the spans
263	/// over which the track plays anything at all.
264	///
265	/// The ramps and the spans are copied out of the plan when the composition is
266	/// built, beside the sink, because that is the one moment all three are known
267	/// — `Playback`'s timer must not go looking for a plan track by id thirty
268	/// times a second.
269	///
270	/// **A sink has no age** (#65). It holds the LAST buffer its tap measured, and
271	/// nothing replaces that buffer over an empty stretch of the composition track
272	/// — past a short clip's end, or while the other format family of a
273	/// mixed-format plan track plays — so a reading taken from the sinks alone
274	/// kept a finished clip's level lit. `sounding` is what says the buffer is
275	/// current: `mix` counts a track only while one of its OWN spans holds the
276	/// tick.
277	struct LevelMeterTrack {
278	    let id: Int
279	    /// The plan's envelope over this track's whole extent — volume, the fades,
280	    /// volume actions and ducking already folded in by `audio.rs`. Nil for a
281	    /// track the plan gave no ramps, which means unity (`audio.rs`'s meaning
282	    /// of an unmodified track).
283	    let ramps: [PlanRamp]?
284	    /// [start, start + duration) of every segment this composition track plays
285	    /// media over — its format family's segments whose source resolved,
286	    /// exactly what `CompositionBuilder.fill` inserts media for.
287	    let sounding: [Range<Ticks>]
288	    let sink: LevelMeterSink
289	
290	    /// True while one of this track's own sounding spans holds `t`.
291	    func isSounding(at t: Ticks) -> Bool {
292	        sounding.contains { $0.contains(t) }
293	    }
294	
295	    /// The meter's reading at a project tick: from silence, in array order,
296	    /// every track sounding at `t` adds its sink's last buffer scaled by the
297	    /// mix envelope over it. `Playback.meterReading()` answers this, and the
298	    /// offscreen harness calls it rather than a copy.
299	    static func mix(_ meters: [LevelMeterTrack], at t: Ticks) -> LevelMeterReading {
300	        var total = LevelMeterReading.silent
301	        for track in meters where track.isSounding(at: t) {
302	            let gain = Float(LevelMeterEnvelope.value(track.ramps, at: t))
303	            total = total.adding(track.sink.read().scaled(by: gain))
304	        }
305	        return total
306	    }
307	}
308	
309	/// The mix envelope a metered track is under, at a project tick — the multiply
310	/// that turns what a PreEffects tap measured into what the mix hears.
311	///
312	/// **One line, and it must stay one.** Phase 5 shipped the search itself here,
313	/// as a second copy of `SilenceDetector`'s, with a comment saying it should not
314	/// stay one; the consolidation moved the arithmetic to `MediaPeaks.envelope`,
315	/// which is now the app's single spelling of the plan's piecewise-linear mix
316	/// rule and the same call the detector makes. Both are asking one question —
317	/// "what gain is the mix applying here", the rule `audio.rs` expresses as a
318	/// ZERO envelope for a mute and a solo — and the app has already paid once for
319	/// two disagreeing project-to-source conversions. This name survives as the
320	/// meter's own way of asking it; nothing about the numbers is decided here.
321	enum LevelMeterEnvelope {
322	    static func value(_ ramps: [PlanRamp]?, at t: Ticks) -> Double {
323	        MediaPeaks.envelope(ramps, at: t)
324	    }
325	}
326	
327	// MARK: - The model
328	
329	/// A subscription to `LevelMeter`. Holding it is what keeps the observation
330	/// alive; dropping it removes the observer, so a view that goes away takes its
331	/// callback with it and nothing has to remember to unsubscribe.
332	final class LevelMeterObservation {
333	    private let id: Int
334	    private weak var meter: LevelMeter?
335	
336	    fileprivate init(id: Int, meter: LevelMeter) {
337	        self.id = id
338	        self.meter = meter
339	    }
340	
341	    deinit { meter?.removeObserver(id) }
342	}
343	
344	/// What is playing, right now, as a level — the one thing a meter view draws
345	/// and the one thing a proof asserts on.
346	///
347	/// MAIN THREAD ONLY, which is why there is no lock in it: `Playback`'s meter
348	/// timer is a run-loop timer on the main thread and every observer is a view.
349	/// The crossing from the audio thread happened in `LevelMeterSink`, one layer
350	/// down, and this side of it is ordinary main-thread state.
351	final class LevelMeter {
352	    /// The instance the app uses. A view observes this directly rather than
353	    /// being handed a meter through the frozen controller and view — see the
354	    /// file's header for why that is the design and not a shortcut.
355	    static let shared = LevelMeter()
356	
357	    private(set) var reading: LevelMeterReading = .silent
358	
359	    /// Which transport is lighting the meter, as an identity rather than a
360	    /// reference: a `Playback` publishes its final silence from `deinit`, and
361	    /// nothing here may retain (or resurrect) it.
362	    private var source: ObjectIdentifier?
363	    private var observers: [Int: (LevelMeterReading) -> Void] = [:]
364	    private var nextObserver = 1
365	
366	    init() {}
367	
368	    /// MAIN THREAD. Takes one measurement from one transport.
369	    ///
370	    /// A non-silent reading always wins and claims the meter. A silent one is
371	    /// accepted only from the transport that holds the claim (or when nothing
372	    /// does), which is what stops a second document's stop from blanking a
373	    /// meter the first document is still driving.
374	    func publish(_ reading: LevelMeterReading, from source: ObjectIdentifier) {
375	        if reading.isSilent {
376	            guard self.source == nil || self.source == source else { return }
377	            self.source = nil
378	        } else {
379	            self.source = source
380	        }
381	        guard reading != self.reading else { return }
382	        self.reading = reading
383	        for observer in observers.values { observer(reading) }
384	    }
385	
386	    /// MAIN THREAD. `body` is called on every change, and once immediately
387	    /// with the current reading so a freshly built view starts drawn rather
388	    /// than blank until the next tick.
389	    func addObserver(_ body: @escaping (LevelMeterReading) -> Void) -> LevelMeterObservation {
390	        let id = nextObserver
391	        nextObserver += 1
392	        observers[id] = body
393	        body(reading)
394	        return LevelMeterObservation(id: id, meter: self)
395	    }
396	
397	    fileprivate func removeObserver(_ id: Int) {
398	        observers.removeValue(forKey: id)
399	    }
400	}

     3	/// The level meter's half of `Playback`: `meterInterval`, the reading and the 30 Hz timer the
     4	/// rate KVO arms and disarms. A pure move out of `Playback.swift`, which sat
     5	/// at the 600-line cap; the stored state (`built`, `meterTimer`) stays there
     6	/// because an extension cannot add stored properties.
     7	extension Playback {
     8	    /// How often the level meter is re-read while the transport is moving.
     9	    ///
    10	    /// It is a READ rate, not a measurement rate: the taps publish once per
    11	    /// buffer, which is 12–20 Hz on the paths this app has measured (4096
    12	    /// frames is 85 ms at 48 kHz), so 30 Hz merely makes sure a new buffer is
    13	    /// picked up within a frame of arriving. `Exporter.progressInterval` is
    14	    /// the same idea at a slower cadence.
    15	    static let meterInterval: TimeInterval = 1.0 / 30
    16	
    17	    /// The transport's levels, right now: every metered track SOUNDING at the
    18	    /// playhead, its last buffer multiplied by the mix envelope over it,
    19	    /// summed — `LevelMeterTrack.mix`, where the fold lives so the offscreen
    20	    /// harness calls it rather than a copy of it.
    21	    ///
    22	    /// **Only a track sounding at the playhead counts** (#65): a sink keeps
    23	    /// its last buffer across an empty stretch of its composition track, and
    24	    /// without that test a finished clip's level stayed lit —
    25	    /// `LevelMeterTrack`'s doc says why.
    26	    ///
    27	    /// **The envelope is the multiply that makes the number post-fader.** The
    28	    /// taps are `PreEffects`, so what they measured is the track before
    29	    /// volume, the fades and ducking — and the plan's ramps are exactly what
    30	    /// `CompositionBuilder` handed AVFoundation to apply downstream of them.
    31	    /// `LevelMeter.swift` argues why the meter must be computed this way
    32	    /// rather than observed from a second tap.
    33	    ///
    34	    /// It is read at the PLAYHEAD's tick, while the buffer the taps last
    35	    /// published is a little ahead of it — the audio path renders in front of
    36	    /// the picture. The two differ by under one buffer, so on a fade the
    37	    /// displayed level lags the applied gain by up to 85 ms, which is under
    38	    /// this meter's own resolution and far under the eye's.
    39	    func meterReading() -> LevelMeterReading {
    40	        guard let meters = built?.meters, !meters.isEmpty else { return .silent }
    41	        return LevelMeterTrack.mix(meters, at: currentTime)
    42	    }
    43	
    44	    /// Armed by the rate KVO when the transport starts moving. A run-loop
    45	    /// `Timer`, not a dispatch source, for the reason `Playback.swift`'s header gives
    46	    /// for the debounce: it cancels deterministically, and app/CLAUDE.md's
    47	    /// five `DispatchQueue` seams are not to grow a sixth.
    48	    func startMetering() {
    49	        guard meterTimer == nil else { return }
    50	        meterTimer = Timer.scheduledTimer(
    51	            withTimeInterval: Playback.meterInterval, repeats: true
    52	        ) { [weak self] _ in
    53	            guard let self = self else { return }

effective peak (format 22, §11 HD-12) joins it as `peak` — `{"peak":
  4000}` alone, or beside `log`/`gamut` or `lut` — whenever the media has a
  reading or an override; a PQ file whose import read nothing publishes no
  `input`, so its plan is the text it was.
- **A/B assignment.** Per timeline track, clips in start order; each goes
  to the first composition track (of that timeline track's set) whose last
  segment ends at or before the clip's start; a new one is added when
  none does. With the overlap rule (§6) that is at most two per timeline
  track — except for a nest clip, which stands for a whole stack and needs
  as many as the nest's own tracks do. Composition track ids are stable
  small integers (video 1…, audio **1001…**) and Swift creates tracks with
  `preferredTrackID:` equal to them, so the recipe can name a track by the
  same id. The two ranges are far apart because `MAX_TRACKS` is 64 counted
  across the timeline *and* every nest, so up to 128 video ids can be
  handed out; `CompositionBuilder.makeTrack` throws on a collision rather
  than renumbering. Segments on one composition track never overlap; gaps
  are left empty (AVFoundation treats them as no frame). The whole
  assignment runs over the FLATTENED timeline: a clip inside a nest gets a
  segment at `nest clip start + its own start`, clipped to the nest clip's
  extent, exactly as a timeline clip does. **An audio segment goes only on a
  plan audio track of its own `pitch`** (§11 #190, #211, SY-26, SY-39): a
  track is free for it when its last segment ends in time AND has the same
  pitch NAME — one of three: `off` (keep pitch off, or keep pitch at
  0.999 ≤ speed ≤ 1.001, speed ≠ 1: varispeed), `time_domain` (keep pitch
  at 0.98 ≤ speed ≤ 1.02 outside that, speed ≠ 1) and `spectral` (keep
  pitch anywhere else) — so every plan audio track has ONE `pitch`, Swift's
  first-segment read of the algorithm holds, and each clip's own pitch
  setting is honoured. A
  clip's "own track" for the ducking rule below is its COMPOSITION track,
  so this split can move an abutting neighbour of the other pitch mode out
  from under that exemption: a ducking clip now ducks it by its extent and
  release (accepted, §11 #190). **Above ×12 a clip has no audio segment at
  all**, in either pitch mode (`AUDIO_SPEED_MAX`, published by
  `rc_speed_limits`), because an export's loudness pass never finishes once
  a clip's audio plays much faster; its video segment, the recipe and the
  file are unchanged. **An audio plan track is split by
  source FORMAT in Swift** (§11 R2-1): `CompositionBuilder` puts each
  distinct source audio format of one plan audio track on a composition
  track of its own — the first keeps the plan's id, later ones take ids past
  every plan id and the placeholder's — because the preview's tapped item
  does not play a track that changes format; the plan does not change.
  **A composition audio track none of whose segments has a source** (missing
  media, a pending reverse or ramp render) holds the bundled `Silence.caf`
  back to back over [0, its last segment's end), never scaled, in place of
  its empty edits, which an export cannot read (§11 #336).
- **Speed / freeze.** `duration != source_duration` means Swift inserts
  the source range then `scaleTimeRange` to `duration`. A `still` clip is
  a segment whose `source_duration` is exactly one source frame — the
  freeze-frame idiom; no image extraction needed. **An audio segment's
  insert is moved by its composition track's leads**
  (`CompositionBuilder.placement(of:shift:)`, §11 SY-24, SY-25): a
  time-scaled segment on an `off` track reads its source 575 ticks (46
  samples) earlier, and a track whose tap runs noise reduction has its
  media placed 6,400 ticks (512 samples) earlier; a lead that would reach
  before the track's 0 or the source's 0 cuts the segment's head to empty
  time instead. **A non-48 kHz source's audio, or an MP3 whose encoder delay
  Core Audio leaves in, is read from a 48 kHz copy** (`AudioRateCopy`, §11
  as before, byte for byte. `rc_project_source_map` (§7.1, §11 SR-20) answers that segment's
  `map` for Swift's readers, unlifted, and a constant clip's two points.
- **Audio envelopes** are per composition audio track, piecewise-linear,
  covering the track's whole extent, with fades, volume, volume actions
  (sampled at 1/30 s across their span), ducking (every other clip's
  envelope multiplied by `level` over the ducking clip's extent with
  linear attack/release ramps) and — format version 7 — the **transition
  crossfade** already folded in, **multiplied by the same
  quantities for every nest clip the segment is inside** — turning a nest
  down turns everything in it down, and muting one silences it. Muted
  clips and muted tracks produce a 0 envelope, and so does a track
  silenced by a solo: while any track in a container's track set — the
  timeline's, or one nest's own — has `solo`, every track in that set
  without it is treated as muted, and mute wins (a track both muted and
  soloed stays silent). The rule is on the set, not on what plays: a
  soloed track holding nothing audible still silences the rest. Audio
  only, and an envelope exactly like mute — the plan's segments,
  `plays_audio` and `assign` never see it, so a solo changes ramps and
  nothing else (which the app rebuilds on, as it does a mute or a
  volume change: the ramps are part of the plan JSON §7.6 compares); a
  solo inside a nest
  is judged among that nest's tracks alone, and a timeline solo on some
  other track silences a whole nest through the nest clip's own stage, by
  the same multiply.
  **The crossfade** (format version 7) is one more factor in that product:
  an overlap whose `transition_in.audio` is true multiplies the outgoing
  clip by `cos(p·π/2)` and the incoming one by `sin(p·π/2)`, over the same
  EASED progress §7.3 hands the compositor. Constant power rather than
  equal gain because the two clips of a transition are uncorrelated
  material, where `cos² + sin² = 1` holds the level and a linear pair dips
  3 dB (§11, R5-2). It is sampled across the overlap on the action loop's
  own grid — 1/30 s, widened so one span can never contribute more than
  4096 breakpoints — because neither the sine law nor an eased progress is
  a straight line. Mute, solo, ducking, volume and the fades all keep their
  precedence, since the term multiplies rather than replacing anything, and
  a pair where only one clip has sound still fades that one. **Every STAGE
  multiplies its own term**, which is where the sound parts company with
  the picture: a clip inside an overlap inside a nest that is itself in a
  transition gets BOTH fades, where §7.3's recipe picks the clip's own
  transition and stops. That is right for sound — both fades are audible —
  and it is deliberate rather than an oversight in one of the two.
  **`mono` is not in the plan at all** and never was:
  `AVMutableAudioMixInputParameters` applies gain over time and cannot
  combine channels, so the flag this paragraph used to promise ("a
  per-segment flag Swift applies with `AVMutableAudioMixInputParameters`
  where possible") described something the API cannot do — and nothing
  applied it, from M2 until road map 2's phase 5. It is sample work, so it
  travels the way pan, the compressor and noise reduction do (§4.3): per
  clip, beside the plan, into the processing tap, where it is the head of
  the Mix stage. A project that saved `mono: true` before phase 5 does now
  sound different, which is the feature.
  **A composition audio track holds its envelope's value at its own first
  sounding segment (one whose source resolved; #217) from time 0** (Swift,
  `CompositionBuilder.volumeLegs`, #87), a second source format's track
  included, because AVFoundation starts a mix input at 1.0 and slews every
  volume change at full scale per 1200 frames.

# Spike S3 — tracks and the master in the preview (road map "audio", AP0)

Run 2026-10-30 against the tree at `9e47f56`, on macOS 26.5.1 (25F80), SDK 26.2. Every code
citation is `file:line` at `9e47f56`. Experiments are standalone `swiftc -O` tools (and one
scratch Rust test over a copy of the core) under this folder; nothing in the repo was edited,
no `make`, Frame Job never launched.

## The rule, fixed before the run

Each question is answered by code citation or by measurement, never by reading API names alone.
The criteria, written down before any experiment ran:

1. **Mapping.** "One composition audio track carries clips of two timeline tracks" is answered
   YES only by a plan the core itself emits (a scratch test over the 9e47f56 core) showing one
   `audio_tracks` entry whose segments come from clips of two different tracks; NO only by a
   code path that makes it impossible. Top-level timeline tracks and a nest's inner tracks are
   answered separately.
2. **Per-composition-track approximation.** Linear stages are argued from algebra and checked
   numerically (error under −120 dB relative is "exact"). For dynamics the error of the chain run
   per composition track against the chain run on the track's sum is measured on a constant-power
   crossfade (the core's own law, `audio_crossfade.rs`) with the app's compressor copied
   verbatim (`AudioDSP.swift`) and a lookahead true-peak limiter at −1 dBTP. Reported: the output
   peak against the ceiling, the worst 50 ms level error, and the BS.1770 momentary loudness
   error. **Acceptable** for a preview if the per-track result stays under the limiter's ceiling
   + 0.5 dB and within 1 LU momentary of the sum; otherwise the preview must say it differs.
3. **A preview master insert.** An option counts as REAL only if a prototype here produced
   processed mixed audio from a composition with taps and volume ramps. Judged on: latency to
   first audio after play and after a seek (target ≤ 150 ms, AVPlayer's own order), drift against
   the AVPlayer over ≥ 60 s (target: bounded, under 1 frame at 30 fps = 33 ms after an hour, so
   ≤ 9 ppm unbounded drift or a shared clock), and how many app files it touches. An API is
   counted as existing only when it is in the macOS 26.2 SDK headers.
4. **True-mix meter.** The reconstruction from per-track taps passes if its BS.1770 momentary and
   short-term loudness are within 0.1 LU of the same measurement on the mix AVFoundation itself
   produces (`AVAssetReaderAudioMixOutput`, the export's read), on material that includes
   correlated tracks, a mono track and volume ramps; and only if the taps' callback order and
   timestamps make a lock-free real-time accumulation possible (one thread, aligned times).
5. **Stems.** A multitrack movie "works" if `AVAssetWriter` writes N audio tracks, `AVURLAsset`
   and `ffprobe` both list N audio tracks with the right lengths and contents (each track decoded
   and compared to its source), and the enabled flags say what a player will play.
